questions.question: Which of the following is NOT one of the three topics the 'This chapter covers' box lists for Chapter 1?
options: High-level definitions of fundamental concepts
A soft introduction to the principles behind machine learning
Deep learning's rising popularity and future potential
A step-by-step tutorial on building a Keras model
questions.answer: A step-by-step tutorial on building a Keras model
questions.explanation: The box lists exactly three items: definitions of fundamental concepts, a soft introduction to the principles behind machine learning, and deep learning's rising popularity and future potential. Hands-on Keras tutorials begin in later chapters, not in Chapter 1.

questions.question: According to the opening paragraph, why is it important for a machine learning practitioner to 'recognize the signal amid the noise'?
questions.answer: So that they can tell world-changing developments from overhyped press releases.
questions.explanation: The paragraph states this directly: amid intense media hype about AI, a practitioner needs to be able to distinguish genuinely significant developments from exaggerated claims.

questions.question: The paragraph describes two opposite ways the AI future is painted in the media. What are they, and what do the authors suggest about both?
questions.answer: A grim future and a utopian one (e.g. scarce human jobs, most economic activity handled by robots or AI agents). The authors treat both as part of the hype that a practitioner must learn to see through, rather than endorsing either.
questions.explanation: The text says the future is 'sometimes painted in a grim light and other times as utopian'. Immediately afterwards it insists on recognizing the signal amid the noise, implying both extremes are more noise than signal until judged against what the technology can actually do.

questions.question: What role do the authors say the reader will have after finishing the book?
questions.answer: They will be one of the people who can develop these AI systems — an active participant in shaping the future, not just an observer.
questions.explanation: The paragraph says 'Our future is at stake, and it's one in which you have an active role to play: after reading this book, you'll be one of those who can develop these AI systems.'

questions.question: Before reading on: write down, in one sentence each, your current understanding of 'artificial intelligence', 'machine learning' and 'deep learning'. After reading p.26–31, compare your definitions with the book's.
questions.answer: Open-ended. The book's definitions: AI is the effort to automate intellectual tasks normally performed by humans; machine learning is a subfield of AI in which programs (models) are learned from data rather than hand-written; deep learning is a branch of machine learning using successive layers of learned representations.
questions.explanation: Self-assessment: the chapter's first objective is to give high-level definitions of these fundamental concepts. Recording your prior beliefs makes the definitions on the following pages easier to retain and reveals which common misconceptions you held.

questions.question: According to figure 1.1, which statement about the relationship between the three fields is correct?
options: Deep learning is a subset of machine learning, which is a subset of artificial intelligence
Machine learning is a subset of deep learning, which is a subset of artificial intelligence
Artificial intelligence is a subset of machine learning
The three fields overlap partially but none contains another
questions.answer: Deep learning is a subset of machine learning, which is a subset of artificial intelligence
questions.explanation: Figure 1.1 draws three nested ellipses with artificial intelligence outermost, machine learning inside it, and deep learning innermost. The second option reverses the inner two; the third reverses the whole order; the fourth describes a Venn diagram with partial overlaps, which is not what the figure shows.

questions.question: Give the book's concise definition of artificial intelligence.
questions.answer: The effort to automate intellectual tasks normally performed by humans.
questions.explanation: This is the definition given verbatim in the last paragraph of the page. It is deliberately about the goal rather than any particular technique, which is why AI includes approaches that involve no learning.

questions.question: Why does an early chess program made of hardcoded rules qualify as AI but not as machine learning?
questions.answer: It automates an intellectual task humans perform (playing chess), so it fits the definition of AI; but all of its rules were written by programmers rather than learned from data, so it is not machine learning.
questions.explanation: The page says AI 'includes many more approaches that may not involve any learning' and gives early chess programs as the example: they 'only involved hardcoded rules crafted by programmers and didn't qualify as machine learning'. The distinction is where the rules come from, not what the program does.

questions.question: Which of the following was NOT among the goals stated in the 1956 Dartmouth workshop proposal?
options: Make machines use language
Make machines form abstractions and concepts
Make machines improve themselves
Make machines learn from large labelled datasets
questions.answer: Make machines learn from large labelled datasets
questions.explanation: The quoted proposal lists using language, forming abstractions and concepts, solving kinds of problems now reserved for humans, and improving themselves. Learning from large labelled datasets is the modern machine learning method; it is not mentioned in the proposal, consistent with the page's point that early AI was not centred on learning.

questions.question: Who organized the 1956 workshop at which AI crystallized as a field, and what was his position at the time?
questions.answer: John McCarthy, then a young Assistant Professor of Mathematics at Dartmouth College.
questions.explanation: The page states this directly when describing how 'artificial intelligence' crystallized as a field of research in 1956.

questions.question: The Dartmouth proposal expected significant progress 'if a carefully selected group of scientists work on it together for a summer', and the workshop ended without solving its riddle. How do the authors nonetheless evaluate it, and what does this suggest about how they will evaluate deep learning later in the chapter?
questions.answer: They judge it by its long-term effect: it produced many pioneers and 'set in motion an intellectual revolution that is still ongoing'. This foreshadows their stance on deep learning — short-term hype and unmet promises can coexist with a genuine long-term revolution (sections 1.10–1.12).
questions.explanation: The paragraph after the quote explicitly separates the unmet immediate goal from the lasting impact. The same reasoning is used on p.39 and p.621, where the authors argue that the hype around deep learning may recede while its sustained impact remains.

questions.question: Can you explain, without looking, why the statement 'until the 1980s most AI textbooks didn't mention learning' is consistent with the book's definition of AI?
questions.answer: Because AI is defined by the goal of automating intellectual tasks, not by learning. The dominant method for decades was handcrafting explicit rules (symbolic AI), which needs no learning at all.
questions.explanation: Self-check on the page's central distinction between goal (AI) and method (learning). If you found yourself assuming AI implies learning, re-read the last paragraph of the page and the opening of p.27.

questions.question: For which kind of problem did symbolic AI prove suitable, according to the page?
options: Well-defined, logical problems such as playing chess
Image classification
Speech recognition
Natural language translation
questions.answer: Well-defined, logical problems such as playing chess
questions.explanation: The page says symbolic AI 'proved suitable to solve well-defined, logical problems, such as playing chess', while image classification, speech recognition and natural language translation are its examples of fuzzy problems for which writing explicit rules was intractable.

questions.question: During which period was symbolic AI the dominant paradigm, and when did it peak?
questions.answer: From the 1950s to the late 1980s; it peaked during the expert systems boom of the 1980s.
questions.explanation: Stated directly in the first paragraph of the page.

questions.question: What did Lady Lovelace claim about the Analytical Engine in 1843, and why do the authors say the remark is still 'arresting'?
questions.answer: She claimed the Engine 'has no pretensions whatever to originate anything' — it can only do what we know how to order it to perform and make available what we already know. The authors find it arresting because it raises questions that are still live: can a computer originate anything, have original thought, learn from experience, or show creativity?
questions.explanation: The quote and the authors' list of questions appear verbatim on the page. The remark is the earliest statement of the skeptical position that machine learning challenges.

questions.question: According to footnote 2, how did Turing intend the Turing test?
options: As a conceptual device in a philosophical discussion about the nature of cognition
As the literal goal the field of AI should set out to reach
As a benchmark for comparing chess programs
As a method for training machine learning models
questions.answer: As a conceptual device in a philosophical discussion about the nature of cognition
questions.explanation: Footnote 2 says the test 'has sometimes been interpreted as a literal test — a goal the field of AI should set out to reach', but 'Turing merely meant it as a conceptual device in a philosophical discussion about the nature of cognition'. The other options are not supported anywhere on the page.

questions.question: Describe 'the usual way to make a computer do useful work' as stated at the bottom of the page.
questions.answer: A human programmer writes down rules — a computer program — that are followed to turn input data into appropriate answers, just as Lovelace wrote step-by-step instructions for the Analytical Engine.
questions.explanation: This sentence defines the classical programming paradigm that figure 1.2 on p.28 contrasts with machine learning, where the machine derives the rules from data and answers.

questions.question: Why were fuzzy problems like image classification intractable for symbolic AI, and how does that explain the rise of machine learning?
questions.answer: Because nobody can write down explicit rules that map raw pixels (or audio, or sentences) to the right answer — the structure is statistical and too complex to enumerate. Machine learning sidesteps the need to write the rules by letting the system derive them from examples with known answers.
questions.explanation: The page says 'it turned out to be intractable to figure out explicit rules' for such problems and that 'a new approach arose to take symbolic AI's place: machine learning'. The mechanism — data and answers in, rules out — is given on p.28.

questions.question: Without looking back, can you name the machines in the lineage the page describes (1642 → 1830s–40s) and who built each?
questions.answer: The Pascaline (Blaise Pascal, 1642, age 19) — the first mechanical calculator; Leibniz's step reckoner — a refined Pascaline; Charles Babbage's Analytical Engine (1830s–1840s) — the first-known general-purpose mechanical computer, on which Ada Lovelace collaborated.
questions.explanation: Self-check on the historical paragraph of section 1.3; the point of the lineage is that each machine shifted more of the procedure from the hardware to the user, foreshadowing machine learning's shift of the procedure from the user to the data.

questions.question: In figure 1.2, what are the inputs and the output of the 'Machine learning' box?
options: Inputs: data and answers; output: rules
Inputs: rules and data; output: answers
Inputs: rules and answers; output: data
Inputs: data only; output: answers
questions.answer: Inputs: data and answers; output: rules
questions.explanation: The figure shows Data and Answers entering the Machine learning box and Rules coming out. 'Rules and data → answers' is the classical programming box; the other two combinations appear nowhere in the figure.

questions.question: List the three things the page says are needed to do machine learning, giving the page's example for each in an image-tagging task.
questions.answer: (1) Input data points — pictures; (2) examples of the expected output — tags such as 'dog' and 'cat'; (3) a way to measure whether the algorithm is doing a good job — the distance between the algorithm's current output and the expected output.
questions.explanation: These are the three bullets at the bottom of the page (the third continues on p.29). The measurement is what provides the feedback signal that drives learning.

questions.question: What does the page mean by saying a machine learning system is 'trained rather than explicitly programmed'?
questions.answer: Its rules are not written by a programmer. Instead it is shown many examples relevant to the task, finds statistical structure in them, and from that structure comes up with rules for automating the task.
questions.explanation: The paragraph beside figure 1.2 defines training this way and illustrates it with vacation pictures tagged by humans, from which the system learns statistical rules linking pictures to tags like 'landscape' or 'food'.

questions.question: According to the page, which two factors drove machine learning's rise after the 1990s?
options: Faster hardware and larger datasets
New mathematical theory and Bayesian analysis
Expert systems and symbolic rules
The Turing test and the Dartmouth workshop
questions.answer: Faster hardware and larger datasets
questions.explanation: The page says machine learning became the most popular subfield of AI, 'a trend driven by the availability of faster hardware and larger datasets'. It explicitly says the field has comparatively little theory and that Bayesian analysis is impractical at scale; expert systems belong to symbolic AI (p.27); the Turing test and Dartmouth workshop are 1950s history (p.26–27).

questions.question: Explain the authors' analogy between machine learning/statistics and medicine/chemistry. What point does it make?
questions.answer: Medicine depends on chemistry but cannot be reduced to it because it deals with its own systems with their own properties. Likewise machine learning is related to statistics but is not reducible to it: it works with large, complex datasets (millions of images with tens of thousands of pixels) where classical statistical analysis is impractical, and it is an empirical engineering discipline.
questions.explanation: The page uses the analogy to justify why machine learning has comparatively little mathematical theory and is 'driven by empirical findings and deeply reliant on advances in software and hardware'.

questions.question: Why is the third ingredient — a way to measure whether the algorithm is doing a good job — necessary?
questions.answer: To determine the distance between the algorithm's current output and its expected output; this measurement is used as a feedback signal to adjust the algorithm, and that adjustment is learning (p.29).
questions.explanation: The bullet on this page states the need to measure the distance; p.29 completes the thought by explaining that the measurement serves as the feedback signal for adjustment.

questions.question: Pick a task you know (e.g. spam filtering). Can you name its input data points, its expected outputs, and a sensible way to measure whether an algorithm is doing a good job?
questions.answer: Example answer: input data points — emails; expected outputs — human labels 'spam' / 'not spam'; measure — the fraction of emails the algorithm labels differently from the humans.
questions.explanation: Self-assessment of the three-ingredient template. If you cannot name all three for your task, machine learning is not yet set up for it — Chapter 6 (p.197) makes the same point when defining a task.

questions.question: How does the page define learning?
questions.answer: As the adjustment step: the measurement of the distance between the algorithm's output and the expected output is used as a feedback signal to adjust the way the algorithm works, and that adjustment is what we call learning.
questions.explanation: The first sentences of the page complete the third ingredient from p.28 with this operational definition, which section 1.6 later implements with a loss score and an optimizer.

questions.question: Which task does the page say is simpler in the HSV representation than in RGB?
options: Make the image less saturated
Select all red pixels in the image
Count the number of pixels
Convert the image to grayscale
questions.answer: Make the image less saturated
questions.explanation: The page says 'Select all red pixels in the image' is simpler in RGB, whereas 'Make the image less saturated' is simpler in HSV because saturation is one of HSV's coordinates. Counting pixels and grayscale conversion are not discussed on the page.

questions.question: According to the page, what is the central problem of machine learning and deep learning, and how does the RGB/HSV example illustrate it?
questions.answer: To meaningfully transform data — to learn useful representations of the input that get closer to the expected output. RGB and HSV are two representations of the same image; some tasks are easy in one and hard in the other, showing that choosing the right representation is what makes a task tractable.
questions.explanation: The page states the central problem explicitly and then defines representation with the RGB/HSV example precisely to show that the representation, not the information content, determines how easy a task is.

questions.question: In the black/white points example, which of the following is the 'measure of whether our algorithm is doing a good job' the page proposes?
options: The percentage of points that are correctly classified
The distance between the black and white points
The number of coordinate changes tried
The sum of the x and y coordinates
questions.answer: The percentage of points that are correctly classified
questions.explanation: The third bullet says the measure 'could be, for instance, the percentage of points that are being correctly classified'. The other options are not proposed on the page; the distance between points is a property of the data, not of the algorithm's performance.

questions.question: Explain what the coordinate change in figure 1.4 does and does not do to the data.
questions.answer: It re-expresses each point in a new, rotated coordinate system so that the boundary between black and white points aligns with an axis, making the classes separable by a simple rule (p.30: black points have x > 0). It does not move the points relative to each other or add any information; it only changes the representation.
questions.explanation: The page calls the coordinate change 'a new representation of our data that cleanly separates the white points from the black points' and panel 3 of figure 1.4 shows the same points with the vertical axis now dividing the classes. Since a representation is just a different encoding, information is unchanged.

questions.question: Map the black/white points problem onto the three ingredients of machine learning from p.28.
questions.answer: Inputs: the (x, y) coordinates of the points. Expected outputs: the colours of the points. Measure of success: for instance, the percentage of points correctly classified.
questions.explanation: The three bullets on the page restate the p.28 checklist for this specific problem.

questions.question: Look at panel 1 of figure 1.4. Can you convince yourself that no rule of the form 'x > c' or 'y > c' on the original axes separates the black and white points, and then see why the rotated axes fix this?
questions.answer: In the raw data both colours span overlapping ranges of x and of y, because the bands run diagonally; any horizontal or vertical cut mixes the classes. Rotating the axes so one axis runs along the gap between the bands makes the perpendicular coordinate separate them with a single threshold.
questions.explanation: Self-assessment: the exercise rehearses the page's claim that a task hard in one representation becomes easy in another. The widget on this page lets you apply the rotation yourself.

questions.question: What simple rule classifies the points in the new coordinate system of figure 1.4?
questions.answer: 'Black points are such that x > 0' (equivalently, 'white points are such that x < 0').
questions.explanation: The first paragraph states this rule and says that the new representation combined with it neatly solves the classification problem.

questions.question: According to the page, what is a hypothesis space?
options: The predefined set of operations through which a machine learning algorithm searches
The set of all possible labels for the data
The development dataset used to compute the feedback signal
The set of rules a human programmer writes by hand
questions.answer: The predefined set of operations through which a machine learning algorithm searches
questions.explanation: The page says algorithms are 'merely searching through a predefined set of operations, called a hypothesis space', giving all coordinate changes as the example. Labels are the expected outputs; the development dataset is where the feedback is measured; hand-written rules are what machine learning replaces.

questions.question: Why do the authors say a hand-built rule system for handwritten digits would be 'brittle and a nightmare to maintain'?
questions.answer: Because every new handwriting example that breaks the carefully designed rules forces you to add new data transformations and new rules, while accounting for their interactions with every previous rule; the system grows in complexity with each exception.
questions.explanation: The page describes exactly this maintenance loop after conceding that loop counting and pixel histograms can do a decent job. The combinatorial interaction of rules is what makes hand design unscalable and motivates automating the search.

questions.question: Give the page's concise definition of machine learning and name its three components.
questions.answer: 'Searching for useful representations and rules over some input data, within a predefined space of possibilities, using guidance from a feedback signal.' Components: (1) the search for representations and rules, (2) the predefined space of possibilities (hypothesis space), (3) the feedback signal.
questions.explanation: This sentence appears near the end of the page; each component corresponds to something concrete in later chapters (model architecture, training, loss).

questions.question: In the digits example, what feedback signal does the page propose for identifying good representations?
options: The percentage of digits correctly classified in some development dataset
The number of closed loops detected
The number of rules in the system
The time taken to classify each digit
questions.answer: The percentage of digits correctly classified in some development dataset
questions.explanation: The page says good representations would be identified 'using the percentage of digits being correctly classified in some development dataset as feedback'. Closed loops are a candidate representation, not a feedback signal; rule count and speed are not mentioned.

questions.question: Suppose a learning algorithm's hypothesis space is 'all rotations of the axes'. In the rotated coordinates, a point has x' = -0.4. Using the rule from the page, what colour is predicted, and what does this tell you about where the problem's difficulty lives?
questions.answer: White, since x' < 0. The rule itself is trivial (a sign test); all the difficulty was in finding the rotation — the representation — which is what learning searches for.
questions.explanation: The page's rule is 'black points are such that x > 0, white points are such that x < 0'. Applying it is immediate once the representation is right; this is the point of saying a good representation makes the task amenable to simpler rules.

questions.question: Explain in your own words why machine learning algorithms are described as 'not usually creative', and what that implies about your role as the practitioner.
questions.answer: They only search within a predefined hypothesis space; they cannot find transformations outside it. The practitioner's job is therefore to define a suitable space of possibilities (and a good feedback signal), which is where human intelligence still enters.
questions.explanation: Self-check on the page's most easily overlooked claim. If your explanation did not mention the hypothesis space being chosen by a human, re-read the paragraph beginning 'These transformations can be coordinate changes'.

questions.question: According to the page, what does the word 'deep' in 'deep learning' refer to?
options: The depth of understanding the model achieves about the data
The number of successive layers of representations in the model
The size of the training dataset required
The resemblance of the model to deep structures in the brain
questions.answer: The number of successive layers of representations in the model
questions.explanation: The page says 'deep' stands for the idea of successive layers of representations and that the number of layers is the depth of the model. It explicitly denies that it refers to deeper understanding; dataset size is not mentioned; and the page rejects the brain analogy altogether.

questions.question: Give the book's example of a shallow-learning pipeline and say how many layers of representation it involves.
questions.answer: Taking a pixel histogram and then applying a classification rule — one or two layers of representations.
questions.explanation: The page says other machine learning approaches 'tend to focus on learning only one or two layers of representations of the data (say, taking a pixel histogram and then applying a classification rule); hence they're sometimes called shallow learning.'

questions.question: The authors admit that some central concepts of deep learning were inspired by the visual cortex. Why do they nevertheless tell newcomers to forget about links to neurobiology?
questions.answer: Because deep learning models are not models of the brain — there is no evidence the brain uses similar learning mechanisms — and thinking in biological terms adds confusing 'mystique and mystery' instead of insight; for the book's purposes deep learning is just a mathematical framework for learning representations from data.
questions.explanation: The page separates historical inspiration (the name, the visual cortex) from what the models actually are. It calls the biological framing 'confusing and counterproductive for newcomers' and replaces it with the definition 'a mathematical framework for learning representations from data'.

questions.question: Which alternative names do the authors say would also have been appropriate for the field?
options: Brain-inspired learning or cortical learning
Layered representations learning or hierarchical representations learning
Automatic feature engineering or representation search
Multistage classification or stacked learning
questions.answer: Layered representations learning or hierarchical representations learning
questions.explanation: These two names are quoted verbatim on the page. 'Brain-inspired' contradicts the page's rejection of the brain analogy; the other options are not on the page (automating feature engineering is discussed on p.34, but not as a name for the field).

questions.question: Describe what Figure 1.5 shows, from input to output.
questions.answer: An original input image of a handwritten digit ('4') flows through Layer 1, Layer 2, Layer 3 and Layer 4; the final output is a column of ten cells for the classes 0–9, with the cell for '4' highlighted as the network's answer.
questions.explanation: The figure is a block diagram of 'a deep neural network for digit classification' with four layers and a ten-way output; the labels inside it are Original input, Layer 1–4, the digits 0–9 and Final output.

questions.question: How does this page's definition of deep learning follow from the discussion of representations on p.29–30?
questions.answer: On p.29–30 machine learning is framed as finding useful representations of the data, and hand-designing them (one coordinate change, or digit rules) is shown to be hard and brittle. Deep learning is defined here as learning many successive representations automatically from data — it is the automated, multi-layer version of the same representation-finding problem.
questions.explanation: The page opens with 'a new take on learning representations from data', directly continuing p.29's claim that representations are the central problem; the depth and automatic learning address the brittleness of hand-made representations described on p.30.

questions.question: Without looking, can you explain to a friend in two sentences what makes deep learning 'deep' and why it is not a model of the brain?
questions.answer: Deep learning learns many successive layers of representations of the data — the count of those layers is the depth. Neural networks borrowed their name and some inspiration from neurobiology, but there is no evidence the brain learns the way they do; they are a mathematical framework for learning representations from data.
questions.explanation: A self-check on the two core claims of the page: the meaning of depth and the rejection of the brain analogy.

questions.question: Which statement best matches how the page describes the representations in Figure 1.6 as one moves from Layer 1 to Layer 4?
options: They become increasingly similar to the original image and increasingly detailed
They become increasingly different from the original image and increasingly informative about the final result
They stay the same size but become increasingly blurry
They become increasingly random until the last layer decodes them
questions.answer: They become increasingly different from the original image and increasingly informative about the final result
questions.explanation: This is the page's own wording. Representations move away from the input, not towards it; blur and randomness are not what the authors describe — purification towards task-relevant information is.

questions.question: Quote (or paraphrase closely) the page's one-sentence technical definition of deep learning.
questions.answer: Deep learning is, technically, 'a multistage way to learn data representations'.
questions.explanation: The sentence 'So that's what deep learning is, technically: a multistage way to learn data representations' is the definition the section converges on.

questions.question: What does it mean to say that a layer's transformation is 'parameterized by its weights', and what are weights, in the authors' plain words?
questions.answer: The weights are 'a bunch of numbers' stored in the layer; they specify what the layer does to its input, so fixing the weights fixes the transformation. Changing the numbers changes the transformation without changing the layer's structure.
questions.explanation: The page says the specification of what a layer does is stored in its weights and that, in technical terms, the transformation is parameterized by them; weights are also called parameters.

questions.question: In this context, what is 'learning', and why do the authors call it a daunting task?
questions.answer: Learning is finding a set of values for the weights of all layers such that the network correctly maps example inputs to their targets. It is daunting because a deep network can contain tens of millions of parameters and modifying one affects the behavior of all the others (continued on p.33).
questions.explanation: Both parts are stated on the page (the sentence about interaction finishes at the top of p.33).

questions.question: What metaphor do the authors use for a deep network on this page?
options: A brain made of artificial neurons
A lookup table of memorized examples
A multistage information-distillation process with successive filters
A decision tree with many branches
questions.answer: A multistage information-distillation process with successive filters
questions.explanation: The page says 'You can think of a deep network as a multistage information-distillation process, where information goes through successive filters and comes out increasingly purified.' The brain analogy was rejected on p.31; lookup tables and decision trees are not mentioned.

questions.question: Why does the page say the Layer-4 representation is also the 'final output'?
questions.answer: Because the last layer's representation is the network's prediction: ten cells for the classes 0–9, with the predicted class ('4') highlighted — it is both the last representation and the answer.
questions.explanation: Figure 1.6 labels Layer 4 representations '(final output)' and shows the ten digit cells; the network's output is simply its last representation.

questions.question: Can you sketch Figure 1.6 from memory and annotate it with the two trends (less like the input, more like the answer) and with where the weights sit?
questions.answer: Input image → Layer 1 (dot-like maps) → Layer 2 (stroke fragments) → Layer 3 (coarse grids) → Layer 4 (ten class cells, '4' highlighted); each layer has its own weights that parameterize its transformation; representations grow less like the image and more informative about the class.
questions.explanation: A self-check combining the figure with the final paragraph's point that each layer's transformation is stored in its weights.

questions.question: What does the loss function take as inputs, according to the page?
options: The input X and the weights of the network
The network's predictions and the true target
The loss scores of all previous examples
The output of the optimizer and the learning rate
questions.answer: The network's predictions and the true target
questions.explanation: The page states that the loss function 'takes the predictions of the network and the true target ... and computes a distance score'. It does not consume X or the weights directly (they only affect it through the predictions), previous scores, or the optimizer's output.

questions.question: Name the two other terms the page gives for the loss function.
questions.answer: Objective function and cost function.
questions.explanation: The page says the loss function is 'also sometimes called the objective function or cost function'.

questions.question: State the 'fundamental trick in deep learning' in your own words and identify the component that performs it.
questions.answer: Use the loss score as a feedback signal to adjust the weights a little, in a direction that lowers the loss for the current example. The optimizer performs this adjustment, implementing the Backpropagation algorithm.
questions.explanation: This is the page's wording; the small step size and the 'direction that will lower the loss' are the two essential ingredients, and the optimizer/backpropagation is the named mechanism.

questions.question: Why is the loss score very high at the beginning of training?
options: Because the loss function has not yet been chosen
Because the weights are assigned random values, so the network implements random transformations
Because the true targets are unknown at the start
Because the optimizer has set the weights to zero
questions.answer: Because the weights are assigned random values, so the network implements random transformations
questions.explanation: The page says the weights are initially random, the network 'merely implements a series of random transformations', and its output is far from ideal, so the loss is high. The loss function and targets are available from the start; the weights are random, not zero.

questions.question: Compare Figures 1.7 and 1.8. What exactly does Figure 1.8 add, and what does the addition represent?
questions.answer: Figure 1.8 adds the True targets Y, a Loss function node that receives both Predictions Y' and True targets Y, and a Loss score output. It represents the 'observation' step: measuring how far the network's output is from what was expected.
questions.explanation: Figure 1.7 shows only the forward path X → layers (with weights) → Y' and the goal of finding the weights; Figure 1.8 attaches the loss function to compare Y' with Y, which the page motivates with 'to control something, first you need to be able to observe it'.

questions.question: Why does the page say that finding the right values for all the parameters is 'daunting'?
questions.answer: Because there can be tens of millions of parameters (p.32) and modifying the value of one parameter affects the behavior of all the others, so they cannot be tuned independently.
questions.explanation: The opening sentence of the page gives the interdependence of parameters as the reason; p.32 gives the count.

questions.question: Can you name, without looking, the three components introduced in section 1.6 so far (weights, loss function, optimizer) and say in one phrase what each does?
questions.answer: Weights parameterize each layer's transformation; the loss function measures the distance between predictions and true targets; the optimizer uses that score as a feedback signal to adjust the weights a little in a direction that lowers the loss (via backpropagation).
questions.explanation: A self-check on the vocabulary the rest of the book relies on.

questions.question: What is new in Figure 1.9 compared with Figure 1.8?
options: A third layer with its own weights
The true targets Y
An Optimizer that turns the loss score into weight updates sent back to the layers
A second loss function for validation
questions.answer: An Optimizer that turns the loss score into weight updates sent back to the layers
questions.explanation: Figure 1.8 already contained the true targets, the loss function and the loss score; Figure 1.9 adds the Optimizer node and the 'Weight update' arrows that close the feedback loop. No third layer or second loss appears.

questions.question: According to the page, what makes a network a 'trained network', and roughly how much repetition does it take?
questions.answer: A network whose weights minimize the loss function, so its outputs are as close as they can be to the targets; typically tens of passes over thousands of examples.
questions.explanation: Both the definition and the order of magnitude are given in the paragraph that completes the training-loop sentence.

questions.question: Explain the chain of reasoning in the Simplicity bullet: why did shallow learning require feature engineering, and why does deep learning not?
questions.answer: Shallow techniques transform the input into only one or two successive representation spaces, which is not expressive enough for most problems, so humans had to manually engineer good representations to make the data amenable to those methods. Deep learning learns all features itself in one pass, so the manual step is automated and multistage pipelines collapse into a single end-to-end model.
questions.explanation: The bullet links limited expressiveness (few representation spaces) to the need for hand-made representations, then presents deep learning's learned layers as the replacement.

questions.question: Which statement reflects the authors' position on the long-term future of neural networks?
options: Neural networks will certainly still be the dominant approach in 20 years
Neural networks are a passing fad with no lasting influence
We may not use neural networks many decades from now, but whatever we use will inherit from deep learning's core concepts
Neural networks will be replaced by shallow learning once feature engineering improves
questions.answer: We may not use neural networks many decades from now, but whatever we use will inherit from deep learning's core concepts
questions.explanation: This is the page's hedged claim. The authors neither guarantee neural networks' dominance nor dismiss them; the shallow-learning option contradicts the simplicity argument.

questions.question: Why does the page say deep learning can 'take full advantage of Moore's law'?
questions.answer: Because deep learning is highly amenable to parallelization on GPUs or more specialized machine learning hardware, so growth in available parallel compute translates directly into deep learning capability.
questions.explanation: This is the content of the Scalability bullet on this page (continued on p.35 with batch-wise training).

questions.question: The page repeats the phrase 'a simple mechanism that, once scaled, ends up looking like magic'. What is the simple mechanism, and what does 'scaled' refer to?
questions.answer: The mechanism is the training loop: compute the loss on an example and let the optimizer adjust the weights a little in the direction that lowers it. 'Scaled' refers to repeating this tens of times over thousands of examples (and, more broadly, to large models and datasets, as the Scalability bullet and p.35 describe).
questions.explanation: The sentence follows immediately after the description of the loop and its repetition count; the scalability bullet then explains how such scaling is possible.

questions.question: Can you list the three categories of properties that section 1.7 uses to argue deep learning is here to stay, and summarize the two on this page in one sentence each?
questions.answer: Simplicity (it automates feature engineering, learning all features in one pass and replacing multistage pipelines with a single end-to-end model), Scalability (it parallelizes on GPUs/specialized hardware and trains on batches, so compute is the only bottleneck), and Versatility and reusability (p.35).
questions.explanation: A self-check on the structure of section 1.7; the third category is on the next page.

questions.question: How does the page define self-supervised learning?
options: Learning without a loss function
Learning in which the targets of Figure 1.8 are taken from the input itself
Learning in which a model labels data for another model
Learning that requires manually annotated targets for every example
questions.answer: Learning in which the targets of Figure 1.8 are taken from the input itself
questions.explanation: The page says foundation models learn to reconstruct the content fed to them, which 'means that the targets from figure 1.8 are taken from the input itself. This is referred to as self-supervised learning.' A loss is still used; no second model or annotators are involved.

questions.question: Give the two reconstruction tasks the page uses as examples of what foundation models learn.
questions.answer: Reconstructing a sharp image from a noisy version, and predicting the next word in a sentence.
questions.explanation: Both are listed in the sentence describing how foundation models 'learn to reconstruct the text and image content fed into them'.

questions.question: Explain the causal chain the page draws from self-supervised learning to the scale of modern foundation models.
questions.answer: Because targets come from the input itself, no manual annotation is needed, so models can use vast amounts of unlabeled data; removing the annotation bottleneck of earlier machine learning unlocked unprecedented scale — hundreds of billions of parameters, over 1 petabyte of training data, costs of tens of millions of dollars.
questions.explanation: The page explicitly says doing away with manual annotations 'has unlocked a level of scale never seen before' and gives those three figures.

questions.question: What does the page mean by saying foundation models can solve new problems 'merely via prompting'?
options: The model is retrained on the prompt before answering
The prompt is compiled into special-purpose code
The prompt queries the knowledge representations the model has learned, and the model returns the output most likely associated with it
The model looks up the prompt in an exact database of stored answers
questions.answer: The prompt queries the knowledge representations the model has learned, and the model returns the output most likely associated with it
questions.explanation: This is the page's description of prompting. It stresses that no retraining or special-purpose programming is needed, and the database metaphor is explicitly 'fuzzy', not exact lookup.

questions.question: What two things does 'versatility and reusability' refer to, and what single idea does the page say grows out of reusability?
questions.answer: Models can be trained on additional data without restarting from scratch (continuous online learning), and trained models are repurposable; reusability is the big idea behind foundation models.
questions.explanation: Both halves and the link to foundation models are in the bullet.

questions.question: The page says the only bottleneck for training on huge datasets is parallel compute. Why is dataset size itself not a bottleneck?
questions.answer: Because deep learning models are trained by iterating over small batches of data, so the data never has to be processed all at once; a larger dataset just means more batches, which is a compute cost, not a structural limit.
questions.explanation: The page states that batch-wise training allows 'datasets of arbitrary size' and that the only bottleneck is parallel computational power.

questions.question: Can you place generative AI on the timeline the page gives (1990s, 2017, 2022, 2013–2017) and say what happened at each point?
questions.answer: 1990s: earliest text generation experiments; 2013–2017: remarkable deep learning results on perceptual tasks; 2017: the first edition of this book already had a generative AI chapter; 2022: generative AI rose to mainstream awareness.
questions.explanation: A self-check on the historical framing of sections 1.8 and 1.9.

questions.question: Which generative AI products does the page name?
questions.answer: Chatbot assistants ChatGPT, Gemini and Claude, and the image generation service Midjourney.
questions.explanation: These four are named in the opening paragraph of section 1.8.

questions.question: Which ordering of the three waves of the deep learning revolution matches the page?
options: Generative AI (2013–2017), NLP (2017–2022), perceptual tasks (2022–now)
Perceptual tasks (2013–2017), NLP (2017–2022), generative AI (2022–now)
NLP (2013–2017), perceptual tasks (2017–2022), generative AI (2022–now)
Perceptual tasks (2013–2017), generative AI (2017–2022), NLP (2022–now)
questions.answer: Perceptual tasks (2013–2017), NLP (2017–2022), generative AI (2022–now)
questions.explanation: The sentence spanning p.35–36 gives exactly this order and these dates; the other options permute the waves.

questions.question: Name three breakthroughs the page describes as 'human-level' and one it describes as 'superhuman'.
questions.answer: Human-level: image classification, speech transcription, handwriting/printed-text transcription, autonomous driving (any three). Superhuman: Go, Chess and Poker playing.
questions.explanation: The page uses 'human-level' for four items and 'superhuman' only for game playing; translation, text-to-speech and recommenders are 'dramatically improved' or 'improved'.

questions.question: How does the hype paragraph distinguish grounded claims from 'fancy fairy tales'? Describe the evidence it uses on each side.
questions.answer: It names specific early-2023 predictions (no one would need to work, mass unemployment within a year, 10×–100× productivity) and checks them two years later against observed metrics (US unemployment still low, productivity far from an explosion) — these are the fairy tales. On the grounded side it cites measurable impact: generative AI generating tens of billions of dollars in revenue per year by mid-2025, for an industry three years old, while noting it does not yet dent the overall economy.
questions.explanation: The paragraph's structure is claim → check against data → separate credit for real impact; both sides are supported with specifics on the page.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT among the emerging applications listed on the page?
options: Transcribing ancient manuscripts in the Vatican Secret Archive
Detecting plant diseases in fields with a smartphone
Predicting floods, hurricanes and earthquakes
Designing new programming languages automatically
questions.answer: Designing new programming languages automatically
questions.explanation: The manuscripts, plant diseases and natural-disaster examples are all on the page (together with assisting oncologists and radiologists). Programming assistants like Copilot are mentioned, but designing programming languages is not.

questions.question: In which cities does the page say human-level autonomous driving had been deployed to the public as of 2025?
questions.answer: Phoenix, San Francisco, Los Angeles and Austin.
questions.explanation: The autonomous-driving bullet names exactly these four cities.

questions.question: The authors write 'Don't misunderstand' in the middle of the hype paragraph. What misunderstanding are they heading off, and why does it matter for the chapter's argument?
questions.answer: That debunking the early-2023 predictions means AI's impact is small. They insist the impact — especially generative AI's — is already considerable and growing remarkably fast (tens of billions of dollars a year by mid-2025). It matters because the chapter's stance (p.39) is to reject short-term hype while believing in the long-term vision; dismissing the real impact would be a different error.
questions.explanation: The sentence explicitly pivots from refuting predictions to crediting real revenue growth; p.38–39 develop the long-term optimism that this credit supports.

questions.question: Pick any recent AI headline you have seen. Using the page's approach, can you state what specific prediction it makes, when it could be checked, and what measurable impact would count as grounded?
questions.answer: Open-ended; a good answer identifies a quantity and a date in the claim, names the metric that would confirm or refute it, and separates that from evidence of real but smaller impact — the pattern the page applies to the GPT-4-era predictions.
questions.explanation: A self-assessment transferring the page's method of separating grounded impact from fairy tales to a new case.

questions.question: According to the authors, what is the relationship between belief in near-term AGI and the rise of generative AI?
options: Generative AI's successes created the belief in near-term AGI.
Belief in near-term AGI came first and contributed to the rise of generative AI.
The two are unrelated phenomena that happened to coincide.
Belief in AGI only emerged after ChatGPT was released in 2022.
questions.answer: Belief in near-term AGI came first and contributed to the rise of generative AI.
questions.explanation: The page says newcomers' assumption (first option) is 'actually backward': fears about DeepMind in 2013 motivated the founding of OpenAI in 2015, and OpenAI kick-started generative AI. They are causally linked, so 'unrelated' is wrong, and the belief dates to 2013, not 2022.

questions.question: What term do the authors propose as a more accurate description of today's 'artificial intelligence', and how do they define it?
questions.answer: Cognitive automation — the encoding and operationalization of human skills and knowledge.
questions.explanation: The page states that despite its name, today's AI is 'more accurately described as cognitive automation — the encoding and operationalization of human skills and knowledge'. It enhances computers' capabilities rather than replicating human minds.

questions.question: Explain the cartoon-character vs. living-being analogy and how the authors respond to the objection 'if the cartoon covers enough scenes, what's the difference?'
questions.answer: A cartoon, however realistic, can only act out the scenes it was drawn for; a living being can adapt to the unexpected. The authors answer the objection by saying the key difference is adaptability: intelligence is the ability to face the unknown, adapt to it and learn from it, whereas automation can only handle situations it has been trained on or programmed for.
questions.explanation: The analogy equates AI with the cartoon (behaviour fully authored in advance) and intelligence with the living being (behaviour generated for new situations). The objection assumes coverage can substitute for autonomy; the authors reply that the unknown is precisely what was not covered, so no amount of realism closes the gap.

questions.question: Which two kinds of problems does the page say AI excels at?
options: Problems with narrowly defined requirements, or problems where ample precise examples are available
Problems requiring common sense, or problems never seen before
Problems with no training data, or problems defined only in natural language
Problems that humans find hard, or problems requiring self-awareness
questions.answer: Problems with narrowly defined requirements, or problems where ample precise examples are available
questions.explanation: The page: 'AI excels at solving problems with narrowly defined requirements or those where ample precise examples are available.' The other options describe exactly the kind of novelty the page says automation cannot handle.

questions.question: What did OpenAI's 2016 recruiting pitch promise, and why do the authors mention it?
questions.answer: That OpenAI would achieve AGI by 2020. It is cited as an example of an over-optimistic AGI timeline that did not come true, to encourage skepticism about similar claims made in 2023.
questions.explanation: The page says 'In 2016, OpenAI's recruiting pitch was that it would achieve AGI by 2020!' and then notes that by early 2023 many engineers again believed AGI was a couple of years away, urging 'a healthy dose of skepticism'.

questions.question: Why, according to the page, is creating robust automation so challenging?
questions.answer: Because automation can only handle situations it has been trained on or programmed for, so building robust automation requires accounting for every possible scenario in advance.
questions.explanation: This follows directly from the automation/intelligence distinction: an automated system lacks the ability to adapt to the unknown, so its designers must anticipate the full range of situations it will encounter.

questions.question: Think of an AI product you use. In the authors' terms, which 'scenes' was it drawn for (what skill was encoded from what examples), and can you describe a realistic situation outside those scenes where you would expect it to fail?
questions.answer: Open-ended. A good answer names the human skill being automated, the kind of data it was learned from, and a concrete out-of-coverage situation (new domain, unusual input, a task requiring invention rather than recall).
questions.explanation: This exercises the page's criterion: judge a system by its behaviour on the unknown, not by the realism of its output on familiar inputs.

questions.question: What caused the end of the expert-systems boom in the early 1990s, according to the page?
options: The systems proved expensive to maintain, difficult to scale, and limited in scope.
Government funding was cut after the Cold War ended.
Deep learning made expert systems obsolete overnight.
Marvin Minsky publicly retracted his predictions.
questions.answer: The systems proved expensive to maintain, difficult to scale, and limited in scope.
questions.explanation: The page lists exactly these three problems. The Cold War reference belongs to the *name* of the first winter, not the cause of the second; deep learning's rise came two decades later; and Minsky's predictions concern the first cycle, not the second.

questions.question: What did Marvin Minsky predict in 1970, and why do the authors quote it?
questions.answer: That 'in from three to eight years we will have a machine with the general intelligence of an average human being.' The authors quote it because it is a precisely quantified AGI timeline that failed completely, illustrating how inflated expectations preceded the first AI winter and how similar claims are made today.
questions.explanation: The quote is paired with his 1967 claim ('within a generation') and followed by the remark that in 2025 the achievement still appears far off, with the parenthetical 'as do many people today' linking it to current AGI claims (p.37).

questions.question: Which statement best matches the author's view of the current cycle?
options: A third AI winter as severe as the 1990s is almost certain.
A full-scale retreat is unlikely and any winter should be mild, but the 2023–2025 investment bubble must deflate.
There is no bubble because revenue already matches investment.
AI research will stop entirely once investors lose interest.
questions.answer: A full-scale retreat is unlikely and any winter should be mild, but the 2023–2025 investment bubble must deflate.
questions.explanation: The page: 'we're unlikely to see a full-scale retreat… If there is a winter, it should be very mild… However, it seems inevitable that some air will need to be let out of the 2023–2025 AI bubble.' Revenue (~$30B) is far below investment (>$200B), so the third option is false; the first and fourth overstate the pessimism.

questions.question: Give the approximate annual AI investment and revenue figures the page cites, and state what the author says AI is currently being judged on.
questions.answer: Investment surpasses $200 billion per year (mainly data centers and GPUs); revenue is closer to $30 billion. AI is being judged by executives and investors not on what it has accomplished but on what it is said it might soon become able to do.
questions.explanation: These are the page's own figures and wording; the author adds that much of the promised capability 'will durably stay out of reach of existing technologies,' so 'something will have to give.'

questions.question: Why is the first AI winter called a 'winter', and what general mechanism does the page say produces AI winters?
questions.answer: The name alludes to nuclear winter, since the period came shortly after the height of the Cold War. The mechanism: inflated short-term expectations lead to disappointment when the technology falls short, and then research investment dries up, slowing progress for a long time.
questions.explanation: The page gives both the etymology (in parentheses) and the causal description in its opening sentence: 'when technology inevitably falls short, research investment could dry up, slowing progress for a long time.'

questions.question: The page says 'It's like expecting a better clock to lead to time travel.' What claim about AI is this analogy making?
questions.answer: That improving AI along its current axis (more capable automation) does not change what kind of thing it is: it remains a sophisticated tool, not a sentient being, just as a more accurate clock is still not a time machine.
questions.explanation: This completes the argument of p.37 that today's AI is cognitive automation rather than cognitive autonomy; progress within a category does not produce a different category.

questions.question: Where would you place the present moment on the optimism–disappointment–funding-drought cycle, and which of the page's signals (dollar figures, what AI is being judged on) support your placement?
questions.answer: Open-ended. The authors place it in the phase of intense optimism; a good answer cites the investment/revenue gap and the judgement-by-future-promise as signs that the correction has not yet happened.
questions.explanation: The exercise is to apply the page's historical pattern to the present rather than to memorize it.

questions.question: Which 2025 observation does the page offer as evidence for the 2017 prediction 'help educate your kids'?
options: Homework assistance has turned out to be one of the top applications of AI chatbots.
AI tutors have replaced teachers in several school districts.
AlphaFold is used in high-school biology classes.
Character.ai is primarily used by students.
questions.answer: Homework assistance has turned out to be one of the top applications of AI chatbots.
questions.explanation: The first bullet says question-answering and 'educating your kids' (homework assistance) are the top chatbot applications. The page makes no claims about replacing teachers, AlphaFold in classrooms, or who uses Character.ai beyond 'hundreds of thousands of people'.

questions.question: What historical episode do the authors use to describe the setbacks AI may face, and what is their conclusion about the long run?
questions.answer: The internet industry's overhyping in 1998–1999 and the crash that dried up investment throughout the early 2000s. Their conclusion: 'we'll get there eventually' — AI will be applied to nearly every process in society and daily life, much like the internet is today.
questions.explanation: The paragraph beginning 'The AI revolution, once a distant vision' makes this comparison explicitly; it links the possible mild winter of p.38 to a precedent in which the technology nonetheless prevailed.

questions.question: Which of the following is the chapter's closing principle?
options: Don't believe the short-term hype, but do believe in the long-term vision.
Believe neither the short-term hype nor the long-term vision until AGI arrives.
Short-term gains are certain; the long-term future is unknowable.
AI will transform the world within the next two years.
questions.answer: Don't believe the short-term hype, but do believe in the long-term vision.
questions.explanation: This is quoted verbatim from the final paragraph. The second option contradicts the authors' optimism; the third inverts their position (they are skeptical of the short term, confident about the long term); the fourth is exactly the kind of timeline the authors reject on p.37–38.

questions.question: Name the two scientific examples the page gives for AI accelerating science, and the field each corresponds to in the 2017 prediction.
questions.answer: AlphaFold (DeepMind), which predicts protein structures with unprecedented accuracy — corresponding to 'genomics'/biology; and Terence Tao's expectation that by around 2026 AI could be a reliable co-author in mathematical research — corresponding to 'mathematics'.
questions.explanation: The 2017 quote ends with 'across all scientific fields, from genomics to mathematics', and the fourth 2025 bullet supplies one example at each end of that range.

questions.question: Why does the author quote his own 2017 text rather than simply asserting that AI's future is bright?
questions.answer: Because a dated, specific prediction can be audited: by listing what has come true by 2025, the author shows that the long-term vision — unlike the short-term hype criticized on p.36–38 — has a track record. It also sets the scale of the claim (deployment in everyday roles and science), not AGI.
questions.explanation: The page's structure — quote, 'Fast-forwarding to 2025', evidence bullets — is an argument from verified prediction. The authors want the reader to distinguish this kind of claim from unverifiable AGI timelines.

questions.question: How does the phrase 'when used appropriately' in the Terence Tao bullet connect to the argument of section 1.10?
questions.answer: It frames AI as a tool to be used by human researchers — a reliable co-author, not an autonomous scientist — which matches section 1.10's description of today's AI as cognitive automation that enhances computers' capabilities rather than replicating human minds.
questions.explanation: Even in the page's most ambitious example (AI contributing to mathematical research), the role is assistive and conditional on proper use, consistent with the automation-vs-intelligence distinction on p.37.

questions.question: Write down one AI prediction of your own with a date, as the author did in 2017. Is it a 'short-term hype' claim or a 'long-term vision' claim by the chapter's criteria, and what evidence would let you check it later?
questions.answer: Open-ended. A good answer makes the prediction specific and auditable, classifies it by horizon and by whether it assumes new kinds of capability (autonomy) or wider deployment of existing ones, and names concrete evidence to look for.
questions.explanation: The exercise applies the page's method — dated prediction, later audit — and the chapter's distinction between hype and vision.
